newsitem.title: USA: IBM's OS/2 Warp 4 not seen gaining share.
newsitem.headline: IBM's OS/2 Warp 4 not seen gaining share.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp's newest version of OS/2 Warp, launched on Wednesday, seems impressive, with voice recognition and an Internet browser built in. But observers say IBM still has little chance of gaining share in the operating system market.

"I don't think it will have any impact in the market place -- nobody cares about OS2/Warp," said analyst David Wu of First Chicago Corp. "Too bad, because it is a good operating system, but it is too little too late. The desktop battle is over, dead, burried."
Even IBM executives duck the question of whether or not version four of OS/2 Warp will grow IBM's share of the PC operating system market.

"We are all optimistic about what can happen," said John W. Thompson, general manager of IBM's personal software products. "But our focus is on what our customers want, not the competition," he added when asked if the new OS/2 Warp might grow IBM's estimated nine percent of the PC operating system market share. He spoke in an interview following an demonstration here to launch the new operating system.

IBM is widely viewed to have lost its clout in the personal computer operating system market in the late 1980s when it decided to go a separate way from its then partner Microsoft Corp. Since then, Microsoft has about sewn up its hold on the PC operating system market with Windows, Windows 95 and Windows NT, with an 80 percent market share.

OS/2 Warp version four is the first PC operating system on the market with an embedded Internet browser -- Netscape Communication Corp's Navigator, the first to have built in voice recognition and the first to have embedded the Java Internet applications programming language.
Those are attractive features -- Java, the highly successful language developed by Sun Microsystems Inc, has become the standard for writing Internet applications.
And voice recognition is a technology many have strived for years to develop to usable state -- and IBM's VoiceType technology seems to work quite accurately with regular speech.
But Microsoft plans to embed Java support and an Internet browser -- its own Explorer -- in its next version of Windows expected out before the end of the year.

Analysts and other observers have said IBM's difficulties with OS/2 Warp stem from lackluster marketing of its earliest versions and IBM ignoring changes evolving in the computer industry threatening IBM's one-time hegemony.

"Even something as simple as the choice of the name "OS/2 showed how IBM missed the significance of the horizontal industry," writes Andy Grove, Intel Corp's chief executive officer, in his recently published book Only the Paranoid Survive. "The idea of OS/2, a new personal computer operating system, was introduced in 1987 at the same time as a new line of IBM personal computers called the "PS/2".
Even though it wasn't necessarily the case, the inference was that OS/2 worked only on PS/2 computers," Grove wrote.
"That perception alone might have been enough to limit the success of OS/2 since the majority of personal computers were made by IBM's competitors, not by IBM itself."
